A REAL TRAINING RUN, INSIDE A SIMULATION

From sensor readings to a maintenance warning.

A machine wears down under load. Its sensors provide imperfect clues. The model learns which combinations precede a failure.

  1. Train on increasing amounts of history.Use 4, 12, 30, then 60 machines. All four stages share a separate validation set.
  2. Stop when the evidence supports your target.Otherwise report a plateau or the training budget being exhausted. A higher target may be unattainable.
  3. Check the selected recipe on future machines.Repeat with three training seeds and one identical-seed rerun.

How the simulation works—and what this experiment can prove

The generator advances hidden wear every hour as a function of load and machine-specific wear rate. Crossing the wear boundary causes a failure, followed by downtime and repair. Sensor readings are noisy measurements related to wear and load. The harder scenarios add sudden failures or later sensor and load changes.

The classifier is logistic regression trained by stochastic gradient descent. Scaling is fitted only on the training subset. A warning threshold is selected from a fixed grid using validation. Training stops on a validation-policy pass, eight epochs without meaningful validation-loss improvement, or 50 epochs. We test four training sizes, then rerun the selected size with three seeds and repeat the first seed.

Machine identities and time periods do not overlap between splits. Labels look ahead 24 hours, with gaps between training, validation, and test to keep outcome windows separated. The model does not use machine ID, hour, failure labels, or hidden wear as inputs.

Every score measures performance against this deliberately simplified simulator. It establishes neither real-world equipment reliability nor the safety of an automated maintenance decision. Twenty held-out machines offer limited statistical evidence. Repeatedly changing policy after seeing test results makes this an exploratory exercise; a real deployment needs a fresh, independently held-out test.

Data-size comparisons share a nested training pool; variation between stages reflects both sample size and which machines were added. Reproducibility applies to the same browser/runtime and settings, not other hardware. Learning curves here do not forecast GPU cost.
